   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?

   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?

   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?

   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?

   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?

Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Snowflake has several Rule Breaker traits: a top player in the fast-growing cloud data and AI market, strong recent momentum (up about 40% in 2026 to $306.84 after falling to $118.30 in April) and a valuation many call excessive. It is weaker on being the clear top dog, since Databricks is a close rival, and on consumer-level brand recognition.
summaries.buffett: Snowflake does not fit Buffett's approach well: it has never made a GAAP profit (net loss of $1.33 billion in FY2026), its business is technically complex, and it trades at about 20 times trailing sales with no margin of safety. Its sticky customers (126% net revenue retention) are a plus, but its earnings record is too short and negative.
summaries.munger: Munger would see quality in the platform and its high customer retention, but thinking backwards there are clear failure paths: Databricks and the hyperscalers competing hard, open data formats lowering switching costs, and heavy stock compensation ($1.71 billion in FY2026). At about 138 times forward adjusted earnings he would likely call the price too high.
summaries.lynch: Snowflake is a Lynch-style fast grower with a simple story: more companies putting more data and AI work on its platform, with product revenue up 37% in Q2 FY2027. But its forward P/E of roughly 138 against adjusted EPS growth near 78% gives a PEG well above 1, and it is heavily covered by Wall Street.
summaries.fisher: Snowflake scores well on several of Fisher's points: a long growth runway, steady new products (CoWork, Cortex Code, Snowflake Postgres, Observe observability), a strong sales engine and a technical CEO. It falls short on profit margins, with a GAAP operating margin of -30.6% in FY2026, and on dilution from stock pay.
summaries.graham: Snowflake fails Graham's defensive-investor tests: it pays no dividend, has never had a profitable year, has only a 2020 IPO record, and trades at about 50 times book value. It is the opposite of a Graham stock.
summaries.thiel: Snowflake answers some of Thiel's questions well: it made a contrarian 2012 bet on a cloud-native data warehouse that separated storage and compute, grew from a narrow market into a broad data and AI platform, and built a strong enterprise sales channel. It is not ten times better than Databricks or BigQuery today, and its long-term durability depends on staying neutral among clouds that also compete with it.
summaries.gerstner: Snowflake fits Gerstner's focus on AI-era platforms with improving unit economics: revenue growth of 35% in Q2 FY2027 plus a free-cash-flow margin around 23-24% clears the Rule of 40 easily, and guidance was raised. His valuation discipline would flag about 17 times forward sales and continuing stock dilution.
summaries.druckenmiller: Snowflake shows the earnings acceleration Druckenmiller looks for: product revenue growth sped up from 29% in FY2026 to 37% in Q2 FY2027, guidance was raised to $6.07 billion and analyst estimates moved up. The stock has rebounded sharply from its April 2026 low, but its volatility (down 8.4% on Oct 16, 2026) and high valuation argue against a very large position.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith would admire the high retention and asset-light model but would reject the lack of GAAP profits and returns on capital: Snowflake's FY2026 operating loss was $1.44 billion. He would also see paying about 20 times sales as overpaying.
summaries.greenblatt: Snowflake scores poorly on Greenblatt's Magic Formula because its operating profit is negative, giving a negative earnings yield and negative return on capital. It would not appear on a Magic Formula screen.
summaries.akre: Snowflake has one leg of Akre's stool in part, a good business with sticky customers, but the other legs are weaker: it does not yet earn high returns on capital, and management has not shown it can reinvest at high returns while profitable. The stock's valuation also leaves little room for compounding from a low price.
summaries.pabrai: Snowflake is not a Dhandho investment: there is no distressed price, the business is not simple, and at about 20 times sales the downside is not limited. Pabrai's 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' test is not met.
summaries.wood: Snowflake fits Cathie Wood's AI theme as a data layer for enterprise AI agents, with CoWork and Cortex Code adoption growing quickly and its addressable market estimated to rise from $225 billion to $460 billion by FY2031. It is less a combination of several of ARK's innovation platforms than a pure AI and cloud software play.
summaries.ackman: Snowflake fits only part of Ackman's criteria: it has a strong franchise and high barriers to switching, but it is not yet a predictable, free-cash-flow-generative business at a fair price, and it has GAAP losses. Ackman usually seeks simpler, more profitable businesses.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economics-shared idea fits partly: Snowflake's performance improvements lower customer bills, which it accepts to grow usage. But it rents its infrastructure from the hyperscalers, so it lacks the structural cost advantage of Costco or Amazon that Sleep favoured.
summaries.valentine: Snowflake was an early Sequoia-style bet on a big, painful problem (data stuck in slow, costly warehouses) during a platform shift to the cloud. It still solves a large problem in a huge, growing market, though today it is a large public company rather than an early-stage startup.
summaries.nash: Snowflake passes Nash's trend, growth and Rule-of-40 tests (revenue growth of 35% plus a FCF margin around 23%) and has more cash and investments than debt. But it fails his instant-kill rule because its operating margin is negative, insiders are selling hard (Frank Slootman sold about $97 million in August 2026), and the DCF value is far below the $306.84 price.

momentum.evidence: The stock closed at $306.84 on Oct 16, 2026, up about 40% from $219.36 at end-December 2025 and about 12% above its end-October 2025 price of $274.88, after falling to a 52-week low of $118.30 in April 2026.

g4.evidence: Snowflake is led by former Google ads chief Sridhar Ramaswamy and partners closely with AWS (an expanded deal with a $6 billion infrastructure commitment), Microsoft and OpenAI ($200 million partnership), and is about 92% owned by institutions.

g6.evidence: Commentators regularly call the stock expensive: it trades at about 20 times trailing sales and around 120-140 times forward adjusted earnings, and its 8.4% drop on Oct 16, 2026 followed valuation worries.

simple.evidence: The basic idea, companies paying per use to store and analyse data in the cloud, is easy to grasp, but judging its technology against Databricks and the hyperscalers takes specialist knowledge.

b2.evidence: Revenue has grown every year since FY2021 (from $592.0 million to $4,683.9 million in FY2026), but it has reported a GAAP loss every year.

integrity.evidence: Management gives clear guidance and has beaten it repeatedly, and it bought back $873.5 million of stock in FY2026, but $1.71 billion of stock-based compensation (about 37% of revenue) dilutes owners.

b6.evidence: Its acquisitions (Neeva 2023, Crunchy Data 2025, Observe 2026) extend the platform into AI, Postgres and observability rather than unrelated areas, though the pace of expansion is rising.

roic.evidence: Snowflake earns a negative return on capital, with a GAAP operating loss of $1.44 billion in FY2026.

fcf.evidence: It generated $1,120.3 million of free cash flow in FY2026 (a 24% margin) despite a GAAP net loss, but much of that comes from paying staff in stock ($1.71 billion) rather than cash.

b10.evidence: Snowflake has an accumulated deficit rather than retained profits, and its share price ($306.84) is below its October 2021 level of about $354.

safety.evidence: At $306.84 the stock trades at about 20 times trailing sales and far above a conservative DCF value, so there is no margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: At about 17 times forward sales and roughly 138 times forward adjusted EPS of $2.22, the price already assumes many years of strong growth.

mu5.evidence: Its sticky enterprise base limits sudden collapse, but there are several ways it could weaken: Databricks taking AI workloads, hyperscalers bundling cheaper services, open formats like Iceberg lowering lock-in, and dependence on AWS for infrastructure.

reinvest.evidence: It has a big runway to reinvest in AI products and new markets (TAM estimated at $460 billion by FY2031), but it has not yet shown high returns on that reinvestment on a GAAP basis.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear fast grower with a simple story: companies moving more data and AI agent work onto its platform, with product revenue up 37% in Q2 FY2027.

ly3.evidence: Its forward P/E of about 138 is well above its expected adjusted EPS growth of about 78% for FY2027, and it has no GAAP earnings.

runway.evidence: FY2027 product revenue is guided to grow 36% to $6.07 billion, and it is expanding into AI agents, Postgres and observability.

ly7.evidence: Insiders are net sellers (about $22 million over the past 90 days and Frank Slootman's roughly $97 million sale in August 2026), and the diluted share count rose from 337.5 million in FY2026 to 349.3 million in Q2 FY2027.

ly8.evidence: It is a widely followed large-cap stock covered by about 52 analysts.

fi2.evidence: Snowflake keeps launching new products, such as Openflow and Cortex Agents (generally available in FY2026), Snowflake Postgres, CoWork and Cortex Code.

fi3.evidence: Its R&D is producing adopted products: Cortex Code had more than 9,100 customers and customer use cases rose 89% year over year by Q2 FY2027.

fi4.evidence: Its sales force has grown customers with over $1 million in trailing product revenue to 828 (up 27%) and added 692 net new customers in Q2 FY2027.

longterm.evidence: Management keeps investing heavily in AI products and accepts lower gross margins (74% non-GAAP product gross margin guided for FY2027 vs 76%) to drive long-term usage, while targeting GAAP profit only in Q4 FY2028.

gr1.evidence: Snowflake has a market value of about $108 billion and $4.68 billion of FY2026 revenue.

ni10.evidence: It has reported a GAAP net loss every year, including $1.33 billion in FY2026.

gr4.evidence: Snowflake has never paid a dividend.

eps10.evidence: It has had GAAP losses every year and has been public only since September 2020.

gr6.evidence: With no average earnings (losses every year), the share price cannot meet a 15-times-earnings test.

gr7.evidence: It has no positive P/E, and its price-to-book ratio is about 50 (market value about $108 billion vs $2.15 billion of equity).

th1.evidence: Its separated storage-and-compute architecture was a leap over legacy warehouses, but today it is not ten times better than Databricks, BigQuery or Microsoft Fabric.

timing.evidence: Enterprise AI agents need well-governed data, and Snowflake's product revenue growth accelerated to 37% in Q2 FY2027 as AI products like CoWork and Cortex Code took off.

th3.evidence: It started by dominating the narrow niche of cloud data warehousing and has expanded into data engineering, AI, Postgres databases and observability.

team.evidence: CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy is a respected technologist and former Google ads chief, but the founders no longer run the company and he has been CEO only since February 2024.

th5.evidence: It has a strong direct enterprise sales force and sells through cloud marketplaces, with lifetime AWS Marketplace sales above $7 billion.

durable.evidence: High switching costs support its position, but in 10-20 years open formats like Iceberg, Databricks and hyperscaler bundling could erode its role.

th7.evidence: Its 2012 bet on a cloud-native, multi-cloud data warehouse was unique at the time, but the opportunity is now widely recognised and crowded.

trend.evidence: Snowflake benefits from both cloud migration and AI, with management calling AI a structural multiplier for platform consumption.

dr1.evidence: Product revenue growth accelerated each recent quarter to 37% in Q2 FY2027, FY2027 guidance was raised from $5.84 billion to $6.07 billion, and consensus FY2027 revenue moved up to about $6.3 billion.

dr2.evidence: Management targets GAAP profitability in Q4 FY2028 and margins are rising (non-GAAP operating margin guidance raised to 14.5%), but much of this is already expected by analysts.

dr4.evidence: Lower interest rates help high-multiple growth stocks, but consumption pricing makes revenue sensitive to customer budgets in a slowdown.

dr6.evidence: Possible catalysts include the Q3 FY2027 report (product revenue guided to $1,588-1,593 million), reaching GAAP profitability, and AI agent adoption.

dr7.evidence: High valuation, heavy stock dilution and strong competition make it unsuitable for a very large, concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Its GAAP gross margin was 67.2% in FY2026 (76% non-GAAP product gross margin), solid but below many software peers, because it pays cloud providers for infrastructure.

fcfyield.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow of $1.12 billion against a market value of about $108 billion is a yield of about 1%, low even for a fast grower.

gb2.evidence: Its operating profit is negative (a $1.44 billion GAAP loss in FY2026), so it fails this test.

pa2.evidence: The business is not in a setback: growth is accelerating, and the April 2026 share price slump has already reversed.

pa4.evidence: It has $4.33 billion of cash and investments vs $2.28 billion of debt and sticky customers, but its high valuation means a large permanent loss is possible if growth slows.

wo1.evidence: Snowflake is a leading data platform for enterprise AI, with AI agents (CoWork) and coding tools (Cortex Code) used by thousands of customers.

wo2.evidence: Cloud compute costs per query fall over time and Snowflake passes performance gains to customers, but AI compute costs are pushing its gross margin down.

wo3.evidence: It combines cloud computing and AI, but not other ARK platforms such as robotics or energy storage.

wo4.evidence: Snowflake projects its addressable market roughly doubling from $225 billion in FY2026 to $460 billion in FY2031, not many times larger.

ac3.evidence: It does not depend on commodities, but its consumption revenue is sensitive to the economy and its valuation to interest rates.

ns1.evidence: Snowflake passes engine performance improvements to customers as lower bills, but it rents capacity from hyperscalers that can undercut it.

ns4.evidence: AI adoption could strengthen its position, but Databricks' fast growth and open data formats make a clearly stronger position uncertain.

va2.evidence: It solves the large, painful problem of storing, combining and analysing huge amounts of company data, and now of running AI on that data securely.

tn1.evidence: Snowflake is a cloud-native data infrastructure company built for the cloud and AI era, not an older firm retrofitting.

tn2.evidence: The market still often sees Snowflake as a data warehouse, while it is becoming an AI agent, transactional database and observability platform.

tn3.evidence: It is a US large-cap (about $108 billion) software company founded in 2012, outside all of Nash's zones to avoid.

tn4.evidence: It passes two of three: revenue has grown every year and cash and investments ($4.33 billion) exceed debt ($2.28 billion); it is not GAAP profitable but management targets GAAP profit in Q4 FY2028.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was positive in recent quarters ($232.8 million in Q1 FY2027 and $83.8 million in Q2 FY2027) and cash plus investments exceeded its $2.28 billion of convertible notes.

tn6.evidence: Total revenue grew 29.2% in FY2026 and 35% in Q2 FY2027.

tn7.evidence: FY2026 revenue growth of 29.2% plus a 23.9% free-cash-flow margin gives about 53, above 40.

tn8.evidence: In FY2026 revenue grew 29.2% while total costs and operating expenses grew about 20.4% (from $5.08 billion to $6.12 billion).

tn9.evidence: It fails the operating-margin rule: its GAAP operating margin was -30.6% in FY2026, far below 20%.

tn10.evidence: It faces litigation over the 2024 data-theft campaign against customer accounts that lacked multi-factor authentication, though no major regulatory threat to the business.

tn11.evidence: Snowflake provides a cloud data and AI platform that helps enterprises store, analyse and act on their data, and charges by consumption (credits used); customers choose it for ease of use, multi-cloud neutrality and data sharing.

tn13.evidence: Total 75 (borderline): cash vs debt 5 (about 1.9x), revenue growth 10, operating margin 0, short interest 5 (about 5.1%), institutions 10 (about 92%), revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 0, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 10, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year and cash exceeded debt every year, and free cash flow was positive and rose from $81.2 million in FY2022 to $1,120.3 million in FY2026, but the GAAP operating margin worsened in FY2025 (-40.2% vs -39.0%).

tn15.evidence: With negative operating income, interest coverage is negative, and total liabilities were about 3.7 times equity at January 31, 2026.

tn18.evidence: Ramaswamy has a good execution record so far, but he has been CEO only since February 2024, is not a founder, and no open-market share purchases were found.

tn20.evidence: Snowflake beat consensus revenue and adjusted EPS estimates in each of the last six quarters, including Q2 FY2027.

tn21.evidence: Insiders are selling hard while the stock runs, including Frank Slootman's roughly $97 million of sales in August 2026 under a 10b5-1 plan.

tn22.evidence: It has real revenue ($4.68 billion in FY2026), positive free cash flow, and buys back shares rather than selling them to raise cash.

tn24.evidence: At about 20 times trailing sales and about 1% FCF yield, the price implies more than a decade of very high growth, above even its current 35% rate.

tn25.evidence: Using about 30% average revenue growth trimmed to 25%, a 25% FCF margin, 4% terminal growth and a 12% discount rate gives roughly $35-40 billion of value, about $100 per share, far below $306.84.

tn26.evidence: It easily passes the Rule of 40 (about 53), but its forward P/E of about 138 divided by expected adjusted EPS growth of about 78% gives a PEG near 1.8, above 1.
